notes.text: Portions — Out of the sacrifice of his peace-offerings, the greatest part whereof fell to the offerer, and was eaten by him, and his friends or guests, before the Lord. And out of this he gave them all portions, as the master of the feast used to do to the guests.
Shut up her womb — Yet Elkanah did not withdraw his love from her. To abate out just love to any relation, for the sake of any infirmity which they cannot help, is to add affliction to the afflicted.
Her adversary — Peninnah: so her envy or jealousy made her though so nearly related.

When she went-This circumstance is noted as the occasion of the contention, because at such times they were forced to more society with one another, by the way, and in their lodgings; whereas at home they had distinct apartments, where they might be asunder; and then her husband's extraordinary love and kindness was shewed to Hannah, whereby Peninnah was the more exasperated; then also Hannah prayed earnestly for a child, which hitherto she had done in vain; and this possibly she reproached her with. Did not eat — Being overwhelmed with grief, and therefore unfit to eat of the sacred food. Which they were not to eat in their mourning.
Ten sons — Oughtest thou not to value my hearty love to thee, more than the having of as many sons as Penninah hath? She would willingly change conditions with thee.

A seat — Or, throne; for it is manifest it was raised higher than ordinary, chap. iv, 18. Here he might sit, either as the judge; or rather as high-priest, to hear and answer such as came to him for advice, and to inspect and direct the worship of God. Temple - That is, of the tabernacle, which is frequently so called.

Bitterness — That is, oppressed with grief. Prayed unto the Lord - They had newly offered their peace-offerings, to obtain the favour of God, and in token of their communion with him, they had feasted upon the sacrifice: and now it was proper to put up her prayer, in virtue of the sacrifice. For the peace-offerings typified Christ's mediation, as well as the sin-offerings: since by this not only atonement is made for sin, but an answer to our prayers obtained.
Give him — That is, consecrate him to God's service in his temple. No razor - That is, he shall be a perpetual Nazarite.

Continued — Hebrew. multiplied to pray. By which it appears that she said much more than is here expressed. And the like you are to judge of the prayers and sermons of other holy persons recorded in scripture, which gives us only the sum and substance of them. This consideration may help us much to understand some passages of the bible.
Drunken — Because of the multitude of her words, and those motions of her face and body, which the vehemency of her passion, and the fervency in prayer occasioned.

Count not, &c. — Thus when we are unjustly censured, we should endeavour not only to clear ourselves, but to satisfy our brethren, by giving them a just and true account of that which they misapprehended.

Find grace — That favourable opinion and gracious prayer which thou hast expressed on my behalf, be pleased to continue towards me. Sad - Her heart being cheared by the priest's comfortable words, and especially by God's spirit setting them home upon her, and assuring her that both his and her prayers should be heard, it quickly appeared in her countenance.
Remembered — Manifested his remembrance of her by the effect.
Samuel — That is, Asked of God.

glossa.text:
*The day therefore came, and Elcana offered sacrifice and gave to Phenenna,* etc. ((HIER., l. de tradit. Heb.)) These portions are understood to be garments, which on the three feasts, namely of the Pasch, and of Pentecost, and of Tabernacles, according to the custom of that nation, were given to the wives, and to the children, and to the servants

*But to Anna he gave one portion, sorrowful,* because he had no sons to whom he might give more. *To Phenenna,* that is, to the synagogue, *and to her sons he gave portions,* that is, temporal goods, according to that: *He gave them the regions of the nations ((Psal. CIV))*. And because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them, *to Anna,* that is, to the Church of the Gentiles, *he gave one portion,* namely natural wit. Well doth he say.

*Sorrowful,* because *the Lord had closed her womb* for the time of having mercy upon her had not yet come, that she might be made fruitful with spiritual grace. As Phenenna despised Anna, so the synagogue despised the Gentile world. Many of the Gentiles awaited the coming of the Redeemer, as we find in Job, and because they persevered in prayer, at length the Redeemer applied consolation to Anna, who wept and took not food, saying:

*Anna, why weepest thou?* Better to the Church is her own husband, that is, Christ, than the ten sons whom she brought forth from the synagogue, who sometimes loves Christ more, that is, his grace, than those whom she bore carnally.

*And he said to her.* The Septuagint, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ παιδάριον Ἡλί.

*How long wilt thou be drunken?* Man seeth in the face, God in the heart. Heli reckoned her drunken, who looked only upon the mouth: but the Lord had regard to her prayer, who saw her heart. Here, moreover, a form of praying is handed down to us, that we should pray not in much speaking, but in compunction of heart and in the pouring forth of tears: because *a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit, a contrite heart,* etc.

*Heli said, Go in peace,* etc. *And the woman went away,* etc. Dost thou see the woman's faith? Before she received what she had asked, she trusted just as though she had already received it. The cause was that she had prayed with much fervour, without any hesitation. She went away with a mind at peace, as though she had obtained the whole. Moreover God had already shaken all her anxiety out of her mind, being about to bestow what she was asking. Let us imitate this woman, and in all afflictions let us flee to God. If we have no children, let us ask them of him, and if we receive them, let us bring them up with much care, etc.

*And her countenance was no more changed into different things. ((RAB. in lib. Reg.))* Another translation: *Her face fell no more,* because most certainly she believed herself to have been heard.

((ID.)) For in no wise was the Church changed away from the faith and love of the Redeemer by turning aside into different things.

*And the Lord remembered her.* ((ID.)) Because Anna devoutly petitioned the Lord, she conceived and bore. So the Church, praying through natural understanding, conceived the mystery of the incarnation in the heart, and brought it forth with the mouth of confession.

*And she called his name Samuel.* That is, God. The firstborn of Anna, a prophet. Who is this but the Lord's man?

((RAB.)) Samuel, the petition of God, or his name: the author, namely, of his birth is God, because to the barren woman praying he granted a son, who all his days should serve him in the temple.

((ID.)) The Church from the nations, etc., *as far as* with perfect faith in the incarnation she joined herself to the primitive Church from among the Jews.

notes.text: Prayed — That is, praised God; which is a part of prayer. Rejoiceth - Or, leapeth for joy: for the words note not only inward joy, but also the outward demonstrations of it. In the Lord - As the author of my joy, that he hath heard my prayer, and accepted my son for his service. Horn - My strength and glory (which are often signified by an horn,) are advanced and manifested to my vindication, and the confusion of mine enemies. Mouth enlarged - That is, opened wide to pour forth abundant praises to God, and to give a full answer to all the reproaches of mine adversaries. Enemies - So she manifests her prudence and modesty, in not naming Peninnah, but only her enemies in the general. Salvation - Because the matter of my joy is no trivial thing, but that strange and glorious salvation or deliverance which thou hast given me from my oppressing care and grief, and from the insolencies and reproaches of mine enemies.

None holy — None so perfectly, unchangeably and constantly holy. None beside - Not only none is so holy as thou art, but in truth there is none holy besides thee; namely, entirely, or independently, but only by participation from thee. Any rock - Thou only art a sure defense and refuge to all that flee to thee.

Talk no more — Thou Peninnah, boast no more of thy numerous off-spring, and speak no more insolently and scornfully of me. She speaks of her in the plural number, because she would not expose her name to censure. Of knowledge - He knoweth thy heart, and all that pride, and envy, and contempt of me, which thy own conscience knows; and all thy perverse carriage towards me. Actions - That is, he trieth all mens thoughts and actions, (for the Hebrew word signifies both) as a just judge, to give to every one according to their works.
Bows — The strength of which they boasted. Stumbled - Or, were weak, or feeble, in body and spirit.

Hired themselves out for bread — It is the same thing which is expressed both in divers metaphors in the foregoing, and following verses. Ceased - That is, ceased to be hungry. Seven - That is, many, as seven is often used. She speaks in the prophetick style, the past time, for the future; for though she had actually born but one, yet she had a confident persuasion that she should have more, which was grounded either upon some particular assurance from God; or rather upon the prayer or prediction of Eli. She - That is, Peninnah. Feeble - Either because she was now past child-bearing: or, because divers of her children, which were her strength and her glory, were dead, as the Hebrew doctors relate.

Killeth — The same person whom he first killeth, or bringeth nigh unto death, he afterwards raiseth to life. Me, who was almost consumed with grief, he hath revived. The name of death both in sacred scripture, and profane writers, is often given to great Calamities.

From the dunghill — From the most sordid place, and mean estate. Inherit - Not only possess it themselves, but transmit it to their posterity. Throne - That is, a glorious throne or kingdom. Pillars - The foundations of the earth, which God created, and upholds, and wherewith he sustains the earth, and all its inhabitants, as a house is supported with pillars; and therefore it is not strange if he disposeth of persons and things therein as he pleaseth.

Feet — That is, the steps or paths, their counsels and actions; he will keep; that is, both uphold, that they may not fall into ruin; and direct and preserve from wandering, and from those fatal errors that wicked men daily run into. Silent - Shall be put to silence: they who used to open their mouths wide against heaven, and against the saints, shall be so confounded with the unexpected disappointment of all their hopes, and with God's glorious appearance and operations for his people, that they shall have their mouths quite stopped. Darkness - Both inward, in their own minds, not knowing what to say or do; and outward, in a stat e of deep distress. Prevail - Namely, against God, or against his saints, as the wicked were confident they should do, because of their great power, and wealth, and numbers.

Exalt — Increase, or advance the strength. Of his anointed - Of his king. This may respect Christ, the singular anointed one of God, and the special king of his people. In this sense also, the Lord shall judge the ends of the earth: David's victories and dominions reached far. But God will give to the Son of David, the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession. And he will give strength unto his king, for the accomplishing his great undertaking, and exalt the horn, of the power and honour of his anointed, till he hath put all his enemies under his feet.

glossa.text:
*It is enlarged. ((RAB.))* Because the word of God is not bound in tribulations, not bound in its heralds.

((ID.)) Unto Christ, whom the aged Simeon embraces as a child and knows to be great, saying: *Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word, in peace. Because my eyes have seen thy salvation ((Luc. II))*. If I shall have rejoiced in the salvation of God, then shall my mouth be enlarged. Namely, through meditation upon the word of God one comes to the lifting up of the heart, whence: *Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged ((II Cor. V))*. Out of the breadth of the heart wisdom is ministered to the mouth.

*There is none holy.* ((RAB.)) Beside thee, O Lord, because none is made holy save by thee, and though there be those that are called many gods and many lords, yet none of them is by nature that which God is; because he alone is he who saith: *I am who am ((Exod. III))*. For a shadow, in comparison with a body, is not, nor smoke in comparison with fire.

*As the Lord is. ((ID.))* He saith not, save the Lord: *But none is as the Lord,* holy and sanctifying, just and justifying.

*Multiply not to speak lofty things, glorying.* He reproves the Jews and the wise of the world, who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. Solomon: *Seek not the things that are too high for thee,* and elsewhere: *God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: let thy words be few.*

*Old things,* etc. Which pertain to the old man, that is, to carnal converse, seek ye knowledge, which is not save from God: because he himself is the Lord of knowledges, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom.

*Unto him thoughts are prepared.* Because he withdraws himself from thoughts which are without understanding, or thoughts are prepared for him, that is, are made manifest. Whence: *The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men.*

*The God of knowledges. ((RAB., ubi supra.))* He himself knoweth you, etc., *as far as* and they are not from him from whom men are.

((RAB.)) That is, the intention of those who seem to themselves to be mighty, so that without God's help they may be able to fulfil the divine commandments.

*And the weak.* ((RAB.)) They who trust in the goodness of God say: *Have mercy on me, O God, for I am weak ((Psal. VI))*. Weak was the Gentile people, when it was estranged from the testament of God, but now, girt about with strength, when it is clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit, it will be able to quench the fiery darts of the devil.

*They that were filled before hired themselves out for bread.* The Jews, filled before, namely with the mysteries of the oracles, hired themselves out for bread, that is, they separated themselves from God: or they tore themselves away from their own seats, lest they should receive the Gospel that treats of the bread which came down from heaven. Filled were those same who were also the mighty, that is, the Israelites to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, but sons of the bondwoman, were made less, who withdrew themselves and believed not in the Saviour, and in those very loaves, that is, in the divine oracles, savoured only earthly things. But the nations, to whom the law was not given, after through the New Testament they came to those oracles, passed over the earth by much hungering, because in them they savoured not earthly but heavenly things. In the Greek thus: *They that were full of bread were made less, and they that were hungry passed over the earth.*

*And the hungry.* That is, the Gentiles, before in want, now taste the bread of the word of God, since it is sweet. So long have they been fed with the knowledge of God.

*The barren hath borne.* In the number seven the universality of the Church is designated, whence John also writes to seven churches, showing that he writes to the fulness of one; whence: *Wisdom hath built herself a house, and hath propped up seven pillars ((Prov. IX))*. Barren was the Church among the nations, before this offspring which we behold arose. We behold too the earthly Jerusalem fruitful, now made weak: because whosoever were free sons in her were of her strength: but now, since the letter is there, the spirit is not: her strength being lost, she is made weak.

((RAB.)) *Many* in the Hebrew and in the LXX stands *seven.* The Jews say that when Samuel was born the firstborn son of Phenenna died: and that at the birth of each of Anna's sons one of Phenenna's died. But Phenenna had seven: and Anna five. Yet the Hebrews reckon the two sons of Samuel among the sons of Anna.

((ID.)) The barren woman, etc., *as far as* by this his poverty we have been enriched.
*The poor,* etc. Jesus, who for our sakes was made poor, and the Lord enriches the same with the glory of the resurrection.

*Out of the dust.* Christ out of corruption, whence: *Nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption ((Psal. XV))*.

 *Out of the dunghill. ((RAB., ubi supra.))* Out of the Jewish people, in which, when the Apostle had said that he had persecuted the Church, *the things,* saith he, *that were gain to me, those I have counted for Christ dung [detrimenta] ((Philip. III))*.

*With princes.* ((ID.)) To whom it is said: *You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel ((Matth. XXV))*.

*The throne of glory.* By sitting in the equity of the Father, and because *the Father hath given all judgment to the Son, and because of his kingdom there shall be no end ((Joan. V))*.

*The poles of the earth.* Namely the four quarters of the world, in which he has enlarged the globe of the Church, which *from the rising of the sun unto the going down praise the name of the Lord ((Psal. CXII))*. 

Mystically, the preachers, upon whom the globe, that is, the Church, is made firm by their faith, of whom it is said: *Under whom they stoop that bear up the world ((Job. IX))*.

*They shall fear the Lord.* Because he will make his adversary weak. It can also be understood, from the ambiguous Greek, as his own adversary. For when the Lord begins to possess us, our adversary becomes his own; and he is conquered by us, not by our strength, because a man is not mighty in his own power. *They shall fear the Lord.* The Jews, his adversaries, over whom the Lord thundered in the heavens, that is, in the apostles, when he terrified them by threatening hell, confirming his threats by signs: whence many were converted. Or they shall fear in the judgment him whom here, opposing him, they despised, over whom he will thunder, saying: *Go into everlasting fire ((Matth. XXV))*. And lest this befall all, the Lord thunders daily in the heavens, that is, in the Scriptures and the doctors.

*In the heavens.* ((RAB.)) Because the just retribution is to come in the day of judgment, but meanwhile he thunders out of his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Spirit after he ascended the heavens.

*The ends.* The last things of a man: because those things will not be judged which in the meantime are changed for the better or for the worse, but the last things in which he shall have been found.

*And he will give.* That is, to Christ

*Dominion.* That is, the Church, whence: *I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance.* Or dominion, that is, the power of judging, because *he hath given all judgment to the Son.*

*To his king.* ((RAB.)) To the Christian people, to whom he gives strength to rule the flesh, that in it he may overcome the world, who for its sake shed his own blood.

 *Of his Christ. ((RAB., in lib. Reg. ))* Of the Christian people, anointed with chrism: yet the whole body with its head is one Christ. These things Anna the mother of Samuel prophesied, in whom the change of the old priesthood was then figured, and now fulfilled, when the fruitful woman was made weak, that the barren might have a new priesthood in Christ.

notes.text: Every priest standeth — As a servant in an humble posture.
But he — The virtue of whose one sacrifice remains for ever. Sat down - As a son, in majesty and honour.
Psalm cx, 1.
He hath perfected them forever — That is, has done all that was needful in order to their full reconciliation with God.

In this and the three following verses, the apostle winds up his argument concerning the excellency and perfection of the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. He had proved this before by a quotation from Jeremiah; which he here repeats, describing the new covenant as now completely ratified, and all the blessings of it secured to us by the one offering of Christ, which renders all other expiatory sacrifices, and any repetition of his own, utterly needless.
Jer. xxxi, 33, &c.

Having finished the doctrinal part of his epistle, the apostle now proceeds to exhortation deduced from what has been treated of chap. v, 4, which he begins by a brief recapitulation. Having therefore liberty to enter,

By a living way — The way of faith, whereby we live indeed. Which he hath consecrated - Prepared, dedicated, and established for us. Through the veil, that is, his flesh - As by rending the veil in the temple, the holy of holies became visible and accessible; so by wounding the body of Christ, the God of heaven was manifested, and the way to heaven opened.

Let us draw near — To God. With a true heart - In godly sincerity. Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience - So as to condemn us no longer And our bodies washed with pure water - All our conversation spotless and holy, which is far more acceptable to God than all the legal sprinklings and washings.
The profession of our hope — The hope which we professed at our baptism.

Not forsaking the assembling ourselves — In public or private worship. As the manner of some is - Either through fear of persecution, or from a vain imagination that they were above external ordinances. But exhorting one another - To faith, love, and good works. And so much the more, as ye see the day approaching - The great day is ever in your eye.

glossa.text: *And every,* etc. Lest the blood offered by the high priests once in the year should seem to have profited less, and the sacrifices made daily by the priests to make men perfect, he adds this, as if he should say: The high priest, offering year by year, does not come to consummation, so also every priest offers continually, and yet by these things is never consummated.
*He sitteth on the right hand.* Well can he consummate who so deserved to be exalted.

*As to the rest.* That is, concerning that which remains, namely the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked. *A footstool.* Because, even if they now resist him, and seem not to be made subject, then they shall appear to all as subject to him, by whose command they shall lie under punishments.

*And he also beareth witness to us,* etc. The Holy Spirit testifies that he has consummated for ever them that are sanctified, and that in the New Testament God will not remember sins. *After that.* As if he should say: After he had said that which is not of force for our proof, he added other things which confirm both the things we say: namely *giving laws,* which pertains to consummation; *and their sins and iniquities I will remember no more,* which pertains to sanctification.

*I will write over.* He does not say *I will write,* but *I will write over,* because those laws are over the strength of men, in the fulfilling of which none shall suffice, save by the help of grace. In these words it is said that he consummates by virtues, then he subjoins concerning sanctification.

*But where,* etc. Not only can it be seen from this authority that Jesus sanctifies and consummates, but also that an oblation is now, after the time of grace, not to be made for sins, when remission has been made.
*Through the veil.* Our faith is veiled, because faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.

*In fulness of faith.* Our faith is perfect, since none of these things is now visible, neither priest nor victim. *Sprinkled in heart.* By this it is shown that not faith alone, but life with virtue is sought. *Washed with water,* that is, with baptism.
*For he is faithful.* As God is faithful in his promises, so he wills that we be faithful to him in our promises. Let us therefore have faith and confession, so far as in us lies.
*And let us consider,* etc. The perfect man by exhorting others, the lesser by imitating the perfect. Thence the Apostle exhorts to those things which befit faith.

*As the manner is.* He blames those who rend the unity of charity, as though they could not dwell among others because of their own sanctity; who rather ought by their own example to have comforted them. *But comforting.* He comforts one that labours who persists equally in the labour, because the lightening of a labour is the effort, or the striving, of him that labours with him, as happens on a journey.

notes.text: Matt. xxiv, 1; Luke xxi, 5.
Two questions are here asked; the one concerning the destruction of Jerusalem: the other concerning the end of the world.

glossa.text:
*And as he was going out. ((BEDA.))* They shall withdraw from the temple, the Lord, etc., *as far as* it was to pay the penalty, and the buildings to fall in ruin.

*Seest thou these,* etc. But it was divinely provided that, when the grace of the evangelical faith had been laid open throughout the world, the temple itself with its ceremonies should be taken away: lest perchance one still a little child, and a suckling in the faith, if he saw those things abide which were made by the prophets and instituted by the Lord, in admiring a worldly holy thing, should slip back little by little into Judaism. The shadow therefore is taken away, and the truth, declared throughout the world, holds the palm.

((HIER.)) He foretells the calamity of the last time, that is, the destruction of the temple together with its people and its letter. Of which: *There shall not be left a stone upon a stone ((Luc. XXI))*: that is, the testimonies of the prophets upon those against whom the Jews turned them back, as upon Esdras, upon Zorobabel, upon the Machabees.

*And when,* etc. ((BED.)) He abides quiet among the saints: while he detests the madness of the proud. For the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful loftiness of the Church: that mountain brings forth not unfruitful trees, but olive groves, by which light is fed, rest is granted to the weary, weakness is loosed.

*And answering. ((ID.))* From the time of the Lord's passion, among the people of the Jews who chose the seditious robber and cast away Christ the Saviour, neither the wars of enemies nor the seditions of citizens have ceased; but the apostles are warned not to be terrified at the coming of these things, and not to forsake Jerusalem and Judea, *because the end is not at once.* For to the fortieth year was deferred the desolation of the province and the last destruction of the city and of the temple.

*For many shall come.* When the destruction was at hand, many came who would falsely claim that they were Christs, and that the time of liberty was already at hand. Many also in the Church, in the times of the apostles, threatened among other things that the day of the Lord was pressing on. Many antichrists came in the name of Christ, of whom the first was Simon Magus, *to whom all who were in Samaria gave ear from the least to the greatest, saying: This is the power of God which is called great: because for a long time he had bewitched them with magic arts.*
*For there shall rise. ((BEDA.))* All these things before the last and bitterest sorrows, etc., *as far as* who, fighting one against another, make the victory of the Church.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down… waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet’ (vv. 12–13) sounds Ps 110:1 yet again — the seated, finished priest set against the standing priests who never sit, because their work is never done.

echoes.text: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart... for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's new covenant, quoted in full at 8:8–12, returns here in brief to close the case: if sins are remembered ‘no more,’ then ‘there is no more offering for sin.’ The recurrence brackets the whole central section (Hays).

echoes.text: You shall tell them, ‘This is the offering made by fire which you shall offer to Yahweh: male lambs a year old without defect, two day by day, for a continual burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘Every priest indeed stands day by day… often offering the same sacrifices’ (v. 11) alludes to the prescribed tamid, the continual daily offering of Num 28. The endless dailiness Numbers legislates is exactly what Hebrews contrasts with Christ's single seated offering — thematic coherence carrying a low-volume allusion.

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Jesus' oracle that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises the classic prophetic threat that Zion will be plowed as a field and the temple mount become a wooded height. Micah's word is itself remembered in Jeremiah 26:18 as a precedent for temple-doom prophecy, giving recurrence; the volume (a prophet announcing the sanctuary's ruin) is strong and the coherence with Jeremiah 7 below is tight.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to make 'this house like Shiloh' and Jerusalem a curse, the OT template for a prophet predicting the sanctuary's destruction and being put on trial for it. Mark frames Jesus in exactly this Jeremianic role, and the temple-saying becomes evidence at his trial (Mark 14:58), so the figural coherence is high.

echoes.text: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
echoes.note: The threat to do to 'this house which is called by my name' as was done to Shiloh undergirds the prediction that the great buildings will fall. Mark elsewhere quotes Jeremiah 7:11 ('den of robbers') at the temple cleansing, establishing recurrence of this chapter in the temple-confrontation narrative.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Deuteronomistic warning that if Israel forsakes the LORD 'this house will become a heap of ruins; everyone who passes will be appalled' supplies the covenantal logic for the temple's fall as judgment. Coherence with the prophetic temple-doom tradition is strong, though the specific 'stone on stone' idiom comes from Micah.

echoes.text: Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in Yahweh’s temple.
echoes.note: The disciples' marveling at 'what stones, what buildings' inverts Haggai's prophecy of glory for the rebuilt house ('stone laid upon stone'); Jesus' reversal of stone-on-stone may play against the temple-construction language of the post-exilic prophets. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: Jesus delivers the apocalyptic discourse seated on the Mount of Olives 'opposite the temple,' the very mountain where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of the LORD and the mount will split. The setting is freighted with eschatological geography, lending figural coherence to a discourse about the day of the LORD, though Mark does not cite the verse.

echoes.text: One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be […]
echoes.note: The disciples' double question — 'when will these things be, and what is the sign that all is about to be accomplished?' — closely tracks Daniel's question to the man clothed in linen, 'how long until the end of these wonders?' and the answer measuring the time of the end. Mark's eschatological timetable is structured by Daniel 12, giving this opening question strong Danielic coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's glory of the LORD departs the doomed temple and halts on 'the mountain east of the city,' i.e., Olivet; Jesus pronouncing the temple's destruction from that same eastern mountain may echo the departure-of-the-glory motif. Faint and dependent on topographical identification.

echoes.text: He said, Behold, I will make you know what shall be in the latter time of the indignation; for it belongs to the appointed time of the end.
echoes.note: Daniel's 'I will tell you what will happen at the latter end of the indignation, for it pertains to the appointed time of the end' parallels the disciples' request to be told the sign of the consummation. The vocabulary of an 'appointed time of the end' shapes the whole discourse.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely reproduces Isaiah's oracle, 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians... kingdom against kingdom.' The paired idiom of nation/kingdom conflict is distinctive enough (high volume) to mark deliberate use of Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD imagery of internecine collapse.

echoes.text: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
echoes.note: 'The beginning of birth pains' draws on Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon where men are 'in anguish like a woman in labor.' Birth-pang imagery for eschatological tribulation is a recurrent prophetic topos (Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 22:23; Hosea 13:13), and Isaiah 13 also supplies the cosmic darkening cluster echoed later in 13:24, strengthening coherence.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'These things must happen' (Greek dei genesthai) verbally echoes Daniel 2:28 LXX, 'what must come to pass in the latter days,' the programmatic statement of apocalyptic necessity. Mark adopts Daniel's deterministic 'must' to frame the wars and disasters as the divinely fixed sequence before the end.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: 'Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress' supplies the same nation-against-nation formula combined with God-sent 'trouble,' matching Mark's 'troubles.' The Chronicler's portrait of God-ordained civil chaos coheres with the apocalyptic catalogue.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Like a woman with child... cries out in her pangs, so were we before you, O LORD' is part of the proto-apocalyptic Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24-27) that supplies Mark with resurrection-and-tribulation imagery. The labor-pang figure for the people's distress before deliverance coheres tightly with Mark's 'beginning of birth pains.'

echoes.text: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!
echoes.note: 'How you will groan when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor' applies the birth-pang figure specifically to Jerusalem/Judah's coming judgment, the very referent of Mark 13. The recurrence of the labor metaphor across the prophets for the city's doom supports its presence here.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: The warning 'do not be led astray' by 'many who come in my name' echoes Deuteronomy's law against the prophet or dream-diviner who arises to 'lead you astray' (LXX planao) from the LORD. The same planao verb and the testing-of-Israel motif recur in 13:22, indicating Deuteronomy 13 as a structuring subtext for the deception warnings.

echoes.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
echoes.note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of Ephraim's crisis adds to the prophetic stock of birth-pang imagery behind Mark's phrase. Faint, included for recurrence within the tradition rather than distinctive verbal contact.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'Wonders in the heavens and on the earth' before the day of the LORD lies behind the catalogue of cosmic and terrestrial signs (wars, earthquakes); Joel is quoted heavily in early Christian eschatology and resurfaces in Mark's darkening of sun and moon in 13:24. Faint here, marked for recurrence.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations. The precious things of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations' supplies a prophetic precedent for cosmic-political upheaval (kingdoms, shaking) preceding the end. The 'shaking' language returns in 13:25 ('powers shaken'), giving the cluster coherence.

notes.text: For the children — The meaning seems to be, as after the death of Antiochus the Jews had some deliverance, so there will be yet a greater deliverance to the people of God, when Michael your prince, the Messiah shall appear for your salvation. A time of trouble - A the siege of Jerusalem, before the final judgment. The phrase at that time, probably includes all the time of Christ, from his first, to his last coming.
To thee — Thou dost not need me or my service, nor art capable of any advantage from it.

But — I bear a singular respect and love to all saints, for thy sake, whose friends and servants they are, and whose image they bear. This more properly agrees to David, than to Christ, whose goodness was principally designed for, and imparted to sinners.

Sorrows — Having shewed his affection to the servants of the true God, he now declares what an abhorrency he has for those that worship idols. Offerings - In which the Gentiles used sometimes to drink part of the blood of their sacrifices. Names - Of those other gods mentioned before.

The Lord — I rejoice in God as my portion, and desire no better, no other felicity. Cup - The portion which is put into my cup, as the ancient manner was in feasts, where each had his portion of meat, and of wine allotted to him. Lot - My inheritance divided to me by lot, as the custom then was.
Lines — My portion, which was measured with lines. Are fallen - In a land flowing with milk and honey, and above all, blessed with the presence and knowledge of God.

The Lord — Hath inspired that wisdom into me, by which I have chosen the Lord for my portion, and am so fully satisfied with him. Reins - My inward thoughts and affections, being inspired and moved by the Holy Spirit. Instruct - Direct me how to please God, and put my whole trust in him. Night - Even when others are asleep, my mind is working upon God, and improving the silence and solitude of holy meditations.

I have set — I have always presented him to my mind, as my witness and judge, as my patron and protector. Hitherto David seems to have spoken with respect to himself, but now he is transported by the spirit of prophecy, and carried above himself, to speak as a type of Christ, in whom this and the following verses were truly accomplished. Christ as man did always set his father's will and glory before him. Right-hand - To strengthen, protect, assist, and comfort me: as this assistance of God was necessary to Christ as man. Moved - Though the archers shoot grievously at me, and both men and devils seek my destruction, and God sets himself against me as an enemy, yet I am assured he will deliver me out of all my distresses.

My glory — My tongue, which is a man's glory and privilege, above all other living creatures. Rejoiceth - Declares my inward joy. For this word signifies not so much eternal joy, as the outward demonstrations of it. My flesh - My body shall quietly rest in the grave. Shall rest - in confident assurance of its incorruption there, and of its resurrection to an immortal life: the flesh or body is in itself, but a dead lump of clay; yet hope is here ascribed to it figuratively, as it is to the brute creatures, Rom. viii, 19.

Hell — In the state of the dead. Holy one - Me thy holy son, whom thou hast sanctified and sent into the world. It is peculiar to Christ, to be called the holy one of God. To see - To be corrupted or putrefied in the grave, as the bodies of others are.

Life — Thou wilt raise me from the grave, and conduct me to the place and state of everlasting felicity. Presence - In that heavenly paradise, where thou art gloriously present, where thou dost clearly and fully discover the light of thy countenance; whereas in this life thou hidest thy face and shewest us only thy back-parts. Right-hand - Which he mentions as a place of the greatest honour, the place where the saints are placed at the last day, and where Christ himself is said to sit, chap. cx, 1. Pleasures - All our joys are empty and defective: But in heaven there is fulness of joy. Our pleasures here are transient and momentary; but those at God's right hand are pleasures forevermore. For they are the pleasures of immortal souls, in the enjoyment of an eternal God. David appealing to God for his integrity, begs for defense against his enemies, ver. 1-9. Describes their wickedness, ver. 10- 12. Prays for deliverance from them, and rests in hope, ver. 13-15. A prayer of David.

glossa.text: *The inscription of a title.* ((CASS.)) This title is taken from the Gospel, not from the Old Testament. What the title noted, that is, victory and kingdom, belongs to Christ, and that is what is treated of here.

*Preserve me,* etc. The second psalm, which touches briefly on the passion and the resurrection; first, Christ, showing the one nature of man, asks to be preserved, saying that all that he endured has been brought through to the glory of his inheritance. ((AUG.)) Christ speaks here according to his manhood, of whom the royal title stood out in the passion: *Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.--Of my goods,* etc. ((CASS.)) If God has no need of the goods of Christ the man, but Christ the man has all things from him, the arrogance of men is overthrown, and the heresy of the Pelagians, who think that anything is done by their own good powers.

*To the saints who are in the land. ((Ibid.))* Christ has now set out how he prayed; he now tells what good things God did for him. ((AUG.)) *To the saints,* etc., *as far as* and power that I might rise again.

*He hath made wonderful.* ((CASS.)) As if to say, these things I said to the Lord: but the Lord made them wonderful, that is, he made my wills wonderful; and they are wonderful in that those who obey them become heavenly out of earthly.
*They are multiplied. ((Ibid.))* Whereby he made them wonderful, etc., *as far as* which sound together in one note, by which his wills are shown.

*The portion of my inheritance.* ((AUG.)) Let others choose other things, etc., *as far as* but those who choose God as their portion. ((CASS.)) Or, *the Lord* is the *portion,* that is, the share and the reward, *of my inheritance,* that is, of the saints. And *the portion of my cup,* that is, the wage of the passion. For the inheritance belongs to the Gentiles, the cup to the passion, which when drunk gives resurrection. But let no one think himself an heir save he that is illustrious.

*The lines,* etc. ((Ibid.)) As it were by lot, in which is the divine election, as the lot also fell upon Matthias, and each man takes according to his own measure. *In goodly places.* That is, among the saints.

*I will bless the Lord. ((Ibid.))* He gives thanks to the Father for understanding, and for the passion, in which by his favour he conquers, and for the resurrection, and for confession; and these are the things through which the inheritance is restored, so that he is king of the Jews, as the title says. *Understanding,* etc. ((AUG.)) Whereby this inheritance can be seen and possessed. *Moreover,* etc. That is, above understanding. *Even till night,* etc. That is, till death, he hath instructed me, that is, my lower part, the assumption of flesh, that he might drive out the darknesses of mortality which that understanding does not have, because for them it could neither be troubled nor fail. *My reins.* From whom according to the flesh I came forth, namely my kindred: they have chided me with injuries, with temptation and with passion.
*I set the Lord before me. ((Ibid.))* From this draw an example, whereby sins may be shunned: for he who always beholds God with the keen edge of the mind is not bowed down by sins.

notes.text: Every priest standeth — As a servant in an humble posture.
But he — The virtue of whose one sacrifice remains for ever. Sat down - As a son, in majesty and honour.
Psalm cx, 1.
He hath perfected them forever — That is, has done all that was needful in order to their full reconciliation with God.

In this and the three following verses, the apostle winds up his argument concerning the excellency and perfection of the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. He had proved this before by a quotation from Jeremiah; which he here repeats, describing the new covenant as now completely ratified, and all the blessings of it secured to us by the one offering of Christ, which renders all other expiatory sacrifices, and any repetition of his own, utterly needless.
Jer. xxxi, 33, &c.

Having finished the doctrinal part of his epistle, the apostle now proceeds to exhortation deduced from what has been treated of chap. v, 4, which he begins by a brief recapitulation. Having therefore liberty to enter,

By a living way — The way of faith, whereby we live indeed. Which he hath consecrated - Prepared, dedicated, and established for us. Through the veil, that is, his flesh - As by rending the veil in the temple, the holy of holies became visible and accessible; so by wounding the body of Christ, the God of heaven was manifested, and the way to heaven opened.

Let us draw near — To God. With a true heart - In godly sincerity. Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience - So as to condemn us no longer And our bodies washed with pure water - All our conversation spotless and holy, which is far more acceptable to God than all the legal sprinklings and washings.
The profession of our hope — The hope which we professed at our baptism.

Not forsaking the assembling ourselves — In public or private worship. As the manner of some is - Either through fear of persecution, or from a vain imagination that they were above external ordinances. But exhorting one another - To faith, love, and good works. And so much the more, as ye see the day approaching - The great day is ever in your eye.

glossa.text: *And every,* etc. Lest the blood offered by the high priests once in the year should seem to have profited less, and the sacrifices made daily by the priests to make men perfect, he adds this, as if he should say: The high priest, offering year by year, does not come to consummation, so also every priest offers continually, and yet by these things is never consummated.
*He sitteth on the right hand.* Well can he consummate who so deserved to be exalted.

*As to the rest.* That is, concerning that which remains, namely the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked. *A footstool.* Because, even if they now resist him, and seem not to be made subject, then they shall appear to all as subject to him, by whose command they shall lie under punishments.

*And he also beareth witness to us,* etc. The Holy Spirit testifies that he has consummated for ever them that are sanctified, and that in the New Testament God will not remember sins. *After that.* As if he should say: After he had said that which is not of force for our proof, he added other things which confirm both the things we say: namely *giving laws,* which pertains to consummation; *and their sins and iniquities I will remember no more,* which pertains to sanctification.

*I will write over.* He does not say *I will write,* but *I will write over,* because those laws are over the strength of men, in the fulfilling of which none shall suffice, save by the help of grace. In these words it is said that he consummates by virtues, then he subjoins concerning sanctification.

*But where,* etc. Not only can it be seen from this authority that Jesus sanctifies and consummates, but also that an oblation is now, after the time of grace, not to be made for sins, when remission has been made.
*Through the veil.* Our faith is veiled, because faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.

*In fulness of faith.* Our faith is perfect, since none of these things is now visible, neither priest nor victim. *Sprinkled in heart.* By this it is shown that not faith alone, but life with virtue is sought. *Washed with water,* that is, with baptism.
*For he is faithful.* As God is faithful in his promises, so he wills that we be faithful to him in our promises. Let us therefore have faith and confession, so far as in us lies.
*And let us consider,* etc. The perfect man by exhorting others, the lesser by imitating the perfect. Thence the Apostle exhorts to those things which befit faith.

*As the manner is.* He blames those who rend the unity of charity, as though they could not dwell among others because of their own sanctity; who rather ought by their own example to have comforted them. *But comforting.* He comforts one that labours who persists equally in the labour, because the lightening of a labour is the effort, or the striving, of him that labours with him, as happens on a journey.

notes.text: Matt. xxiv, 1; Luke xxi, 5.
Two questions are here asked; the one concerning the destruction of Jerusalem: the other concerning the end of the world.

glossa.text:
*And as he was going out. ((BEDA.))* They shall withdraw from the temple, the Lord, etc., *as far as* it was to pay the penalty, and the buildings to fall in ruin.

*Seest thou these,* etc. But it was divinely provided that, when the grace of the evangelical faith had been laid open throughout the world, the temple itself with its ceremonies should be taken away: lest perchance one still a little child, and a suckling in the faith, if he saw those things abide which were made by the prophets and instituted by the Lord, in admiring a worldly holy thing, should slip back little by little into Judaism. The shadow therefore is taken away, and the truth, declared throughout the world, holds the palm.

((HIER.)) He foretells the calamity of the last time, that is, the destruction of the temple together with its people and its letter. Of which: *There shall not be left a stone upon a stone ((Luc. XXI))*: that is, the testimonies of the prophets upon those against whom the Jews turned them back, as upon Esdras, upon Zorobabel, upon the Machabees.

*And when,* etc. ((BED.)) He abides quiet among the saints: while he detests the madness of the proud. For the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful loftiness of the Church: that mountain brings forth not unfruitful trees, but olive groves, by which light is fed, rest is granted to the weary, weakness is loosed.

*And answering. ((ID.))* From the time of the Lord's passion, among the people of the Jews who chose the seditious robber and cast away Christ the Saviour, neither the wars of enemies nor the seditions of citizens have ceased; but the apostles are warned not to be terrified at the coming of these things, and not to forsake Jerusalem and Judea, *because the end is not at once.* For to the fortieth year was deferred the desolation of the province and the last destruction of the city and of the temple.

*For many shall come.* When the destruction was at hand, many came who would falsely claim that they were Christs, and that the time of liberty was already at hand. Many also in the Church, in the times of the apostles, threatened among other things that the day of the Lord was pressing on. Many antichrists came in the name of Christ, of whom the first was Simon Magus, *to whom all who were in Samaria gave ear from the least to the greatest, saying: This is the power of God which is called great: because for a long time he had bewitched them with magic arts.*
*For there shall rise. ((BEDA.))* All these things before the last and bitterest sorrows, etc., *as far as* who, fighting one against another, make the victory of the Church.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down… waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet’ (vv. 12–13) sounds Ps 110:1 yet again — the seated, finished priest set against the standing priests who never sit, because their work is never done.

echoes.text: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart... for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's new covenant, quoted in full at 8:8–12, returns here in brief to close the case: if sins are remembered ‘no more,’ then ‘there is no more offering for sin.’ The recurrence brackets the whole central section (Hays).

echoes.text: You shall tell them, ‘This is the offering made by fire which you shall offer to Yahweh: male lambs a year old without defect, two day by day, for a continual burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘Every priest indeed stands day by day… often offering the same sacrifices’ (v. 11) alludes to the prescribed tamid, the continual daily offering of Num 28. The endless dailiness Numbers legislates is exactly what Hebrews contrasts with Christ's single seated offering — thematic coherence carrying a low-volume allusion.

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Jesus' oracle that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises the classic prophetic threat that Zion will be plowed as a field and the temple mount become a wooded height. Micah's word is itself remembered in Jeremiah 26:18 as a precedent for temple-doom prophecy, giving recurrence; the volume (a prophet announcing the sanctuary's ruin) is strong and the coherence with Jeremiah 7 below is tight.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to make 'this house like Shiloh' and Jerusalem a curse, the OT template for a prophet predicting the sanctuary's destruction and being put on trial for it. Mark frames Jesus in exactly this Jeremianic role, and the temple-saying becomes evidence at his trial (Mark 14:58), so the figural coherence is high.

echoes.text: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
echoes.note: The threat to do to 'this house which is called by my name' as was done to Shiloh undergirds the prediction that the great buildings will fall. Mark elsewhere quotes Jeremiah 7:11 ('den of robbers') at the temple cleansing, establishing recurrence of this chapter in the temple-confrontation narrative.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Deuteronomistic warning that if Israel forsakes the LORD 'this house will become a heap of ruins; everyone who passes will be appalled' supplies the covenantal logic for the temple's fall as judgment. Coherence with the prophetic temple-doom tradition is strong, though the specific 'stone on stone' idiom comes from Micah.

echoes.text: Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in Yahweh’s temple.
echoes.note: The disciples' marveling at 'what stones, what buildings' inverts Haggai's prophecy of glory for the rebuilt house ('stone laid upon stone'); Jesus' reversal of stone-on-stone may play against the temple-construction language of the post-exilic prophets. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: Jesus delivers the apocalyptic discourse seated on the Mount of Olives 'opposite the temple,' the very mountain where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of the LORD and the mount will split. The setting is freighted with eschatological geography, lending figural coherence to a discourse about the day of the LORD, though Mark does not cite the verse.

echoes.text: One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be […]
echoes.note: The disciples' double question — 'when will these things be, and what is the sign that all is about to be accomplished?' — closely tracks Daniel's question to the man clothed in linen, 'how long until the end of these wonders?' and the answer measuring the time of the end. Mark's eschatological timetable is structured by Daniel 12, giving this opening question strong Danielic coherence.

echoes.note: Ezekiel's glory of the LORD departs the doomed temple and halts on 'the mountain east of the city,' i.e., Olivet; Jesus pronouncing the temple's destruction from that same eastern mountain may echo the departure-of-the-glory motif. Faint and dependent on topographical identification.

echoes.note: Daniel's 'I will tell you what will happen at the latter end of the indignation, for it pertains to the appointed time of the end' parallels the disciples' request to be told the sign of the consummation. The vocabulary of an 'appointed time of the end' shapes the whole discourse.

echoes.note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely reproduces Isaiah's oracle, 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians... kingdom against kingdom.' The paired idiom of nation/kingdom conflict is distinctive enough (high volume) to mark deliberate use of Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD imagery of internecine collapse.

echoes.note: 'The beginning of birth pains' draws on Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon where men are 'in anguish like a woman in labor.' Birth-pang imagery for eschatological tribulation is a recurrent prophetic topos (Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 22:23; Hosea 13:13), and Isaiah 13 also supplies the cosmic darkening cluster echoed later in 13:24, strengthening coherence.

Mark adopts Daniel's deterministic 'must' to frame the wars and disasters as the divinely fixed sequence before the end.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: 'Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress' supplies the same nation-against-nation formula combined with God-sent 'trouble,' matching Mark's 'troubles.' The Chronicler's portrait of God-ordained civil chaos coheres with the apocalyptic catalogue.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Like a woman with child... cries out in her pangs, so were we before you, O LORD' is part of the proto-apocalyptic Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24-27) that supplies Mark with resurrection-and-tribulation imagery. The labor-pang figure for the people's distress before deliverance coheres tightly with Mark's 'beginning of birth pains.'

echoes.text: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!
echoes.note: 'How you will groan when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor' applies the birth-pang figure specifically to Jerusalem/Judah's coming judgment, the very referent of Mark 13. The recurrence of the labor metaphor across the prophets for the city's doom supports its presence here.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: The warning 'do not be led astray' by 'many who come in my name' echoes Deuteronomy's law against the prophet or dream-diviner who arises to 'lead you astray' (LXX planao) from the LORD. The same planao verb and the testing-of-Israel motif recur in 13:22, indicating Deuteronomy 13 as a structuring subtext for the deception warnings.

echoes.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
echoes.note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of Ephraim's crisis adds to the prophetic stock of birth-pang imagery behind Mark's phrase. Faint, included for recurrence within the tradition rather than distinctive verbal contact.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'Wonders in the heavens and on the earth' before the day of the LORD lies behind the catalogue of cosmic and terrestrial signs (wars, earthquakes); Joel is quoted heavily in early Christian eschatology and resurfaces in Mark's darkening of sun and moon in 13:24. Faint here, marked for recurrence.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations. The precious things of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations' supplies a prophetic precedent for cosmic-political upheaval (kingdoms, shaking) preceding the end. The 'shaking' language returns in 13:25 ('powers shaken'), giving the cluster coherence.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Look, Teacher — what large stones, what buildings!
Not one stone will be left upon another.
When you hear of wars and rumors, do not be alarmed.
This is but the beginning of the birth pangs.
Those who sleep in the dust will wake;
the wise will shine like the stars forever.
Come, let us worship and not lose heart.
The day is drawing near. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: The disciples marveled at the temple stones, and Jesus said, Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left upon another.
The day is drawing near.
When the earth shakes and the nations rage, do not be alarmed; this is the beginning, the first birth pangs of something being born.
The day is drawing near.
Those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, and the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, like the stars forever and ever.
The day is drawing near.
So let us hold fast to our hope without wavering, and spur one another on to love. Come, let us worship.
The day is drawing near. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Not one stone will be left standing on another.
We will not lose heart.
When the nations rage, do not be alarmed.
We will not lose heart.
The wise will shine like the stars forever.
We will not lose heart.
Come, hold fast and worship; the day draws near.
We will not lose heart. Amen.
